_notes: Static reference data for the pregnancy tracking module. Educational information only, not medical advice. Milestone timing is approximate and varies by individual/pregnancy. Trimester-level hormone/mood/nutrition data is normalized (not repeated per week) to avoid duplication in the app's data layer — join on 'trimester'.

trimesters.hormoneNotes: hCG rises rapidly (roughly doubling every 48-72 hours early on), peaking around weeks 8-11 then leveling off. Progesterone climbs steadily to maintain the uterine lining and relax smooth muscle. Estrogen rises steadily throughout.
trimesters.moodPhysicalNotes: Fatigue, nausea ('morning sickness'), breast tenderness, and heightened emotional sensitivity are commonly reported, often linked to the rapid hormonal shifts above. Symptoms typically ease as the trimester ends and hCG plateaus.

nutritionFocus.why: critical for neural tube development in early weeks
commonly suggested to help ease nausea
supports rising blood volume and can ease fatigue/constipation
sources: herbal teas cleared by a provider

trimesters.generalTips: Small, frequent meals and ginger are commonly reported to help with nausea. Avoid the 'avoidList' items from the first positive test onward.

trimesters.hormoneNotes: hCG plateaus. Progesterone and estrogen continue rising steadily, supporting placental growth. Relaxin increases, gradually loosening ligaments and joints.
trimesters.moodPhysicalNotes: Often described as the more comfortable stretch of pregnancy — energy commonly returns as nausea eases and mood may stabilize. Some report vivid dreams, skin/hair changes, and round-ligament pain as the uterus expands.

nutritionFocus.why: supports the significant rise in blood volume
sources: pair with vitamin C for absorption

nutritionFocus.why: needs increase to support fetal growth

trimesters.generalTips: This is typically when the anatomy scan (around week 20) happens and appetite often increases.

trimesters.hormoneNotes: Estrogen and progesterone reach their highest levels of pregnancy. Relaxin peaks, preparing the pelvis for birth. Oxytocin sensitivity and prolactin rise in preparation for labor and lactation.
trimesters.moodPhysicalNotes: Physical discomfort (back pain, disrupted sleep, Braxton Hicks contractions) is common. Many report heightened anxiety about labor alongside a 'nesting' instinct in the final weeks; mood can fluctuate with poor sleep and physical strain.

nutritionFocus.why: demand stays elevated through the final stretch

trimesters.generalTips: Total daily calorie needs are typically modestly higher in this trimester; the added calories should come from nutrient-dense food rather than empty calories.

avoidList.reason: no amount established as safe during pregnancy

avoidList.item: Raw or undercooked meat, eggs, and fish (incl. sushi with raw fish)
avoidList.reason: risk of foodborne illness (Salmonella, Listeria, Toxoplasma)

avoidList.item: Deli meats and hot dogs, unless heated until steaming
High-mercury fish (shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish)
avoidList.reason: mercury can affect fetal nervous system development
high intake linked to increased risk in some studies

avoidList.item: Certain herbal teas/supplements without a provider's approval

weeks.sizeComparison: n/a (cycle tracking phase; conception hasn't occurred yet)
milestones: Dated from the last menstrual period; the body is preparing for ovulation.
Ovulation typically occurs around this week; this is the usual conception window.
Fertilization typically occurs; the resulting cells begin rapidly dividing into a blastocyst.
Implantation in the uterine lining typically occurs; hCG begins rising, often enough to be detected by a home test around a missed period.
The neural tube (future brain and spinal cord) begins forming.
The heart begins beating and pumping blood; the neural tube closes; tiny limb buds appear.
Brain and facial features develop rapidly; arm and leg buds elongate.
Fingers and toes begin forming (webbed at first); all major organ systems have started developing.
Embryo is now typically referred to as a fetus; external sex organs begin differentiating (not yet visible on ultrasound); the tail structure disappears.
Vital organs are functioning; fingernails start to form.
The fetus may start small movements (not yet felt); tooth buds are forming.
Reflexes are developing; miscarriage risk drops significantly by the end of this week.
Vocal cords and fingerprints are forming; end of the first trimester.
The fetus can squint and frown; genitals become more distinguishable.
Skeleton is hardening from cartilage to bone; can sense light through closed eyelids.
Early movement ('quickening') may start to be felt, especially in later pregnancies; circulatory system is fully functioning.
Skeleton continues hardening; fat stores begin forming.
Ears reach their final position and the fetus may begin responding to sound; yawning and hiccups are sometimes visible on ultrasound.
A protective coating (vernix caseosa) begins covering the skin; senses of smell, taste, hearing, and sight are developing rapidly.
Halfway point; the anatomy ultrasound is typically done around now; fine hair (lanugo) covers the body.
Movements typically become stronger and more noticeable; digestive system continues developing.
Eyebrows and eyelids are fully formed; sense of touch is developing.
Blood vessels in the lungs are developing in preparation for breathing; skin is still somewhat translucent.
Often cited as a viability milestone with intensive medical care; the inner ear has developed, aiding balance.
The fetus responds to touch and sound; hair color and texture are forming.
Eyes begin to open; lungs are developing surfactant needed for breathing air.
End of the second trimester; brain tissue develops rapidly; sleep-wake cycles begin emerging.
Third trimester begins; the fetus can blink and has eyelashes; rapid brain growth continues.
Muscles and lungs continue maturing; kicks and movements typically feel stronger.
Brain is developing more grooves and surface area.
The fetus can turn its head side to side; all five senses are functioning.
Practice breathing movements occur; bones are fully formed but still soft and flexible.
The immune system is developing with antibodies passed from the mother.
Central nervous system and lungs continue maturing; fingernails reach the fingertips.
Kidneys are fully developed; most structural development is complete, with weight gain being the main focus from here.
The protective vernix and lanugo begin shedding; the head may start engaging in the pelvis.
Considered 'early term'; continued fat gain supports temperature regulation after birth.
Organs are essentially mature and ready for birth; brain development continues rapidly.
Considered full term; lungs are among the last organs to fully mature.
Estimated due date; average size is roughly 7.5 lb / 51 cm, though the normal range varies widely.
